v.why: Raising an already large learning rate causes divergence and collapse in accuracy (e.g. exp 7).
Reducing a very large learning rate restores stable training, giving large gains (exps 8, 17, 18).
Very strong L2 penalty over-regularizes and underfits the network (exps 83, 99).
Relaxing an excessive L2 penalty frees the model to fit, with big gains (exps 89, 90, 99, 100).
Deeper networks are more unstable at high learning rates and diverge (exps 47, 55).
Shallower networks tolerate high learning rates better, so removing depth helps (exps 48, 56, 60).
With a tiny learning rate, wider layers add capacity and effective update speed, helping the underfit model (exps 25, 33).
At low learning rates there is no instability, so additional depth adds useful capacity (exp 54).
Very small batches give noisy gradients, so moving to larger batches stabilizes training (exp 68).
A tiny learning rate underfits within 243 epochs, so increasing it speeds convergence.

raw:
These ten hypotheses rest on the 100 single-seed experiments plus my priors about MLP training, not on the full tabulated benchmark. The strongest evidence is for the high-learning-rate and high-alpha effects. The last three (lr up at low lr, width up at low lr, batch up at low batch) are the weakest, since the experiments there are mixed or sparse.

- **High learning rate:** Stepping the rate up diverges (exp 7: -14.6, -71.4, -38.8). Stepping it down recovers (exps 8, 17, 18). Adding depth also hurts there (exps 47, 55), and removing depth helps (exps 48, 56, 60).
- **High alpha:** Raising alpha is clearly harmful (exps 83, 99). Lowering it helps (exps 89, 90, 99, 100).
- **Low learning rate:** The network is underfit, so extra capacity helps. Width up gains in exps 25 and 33, and depth up gains in exp 54.
- **Low batch size:** Larger batches smooth noisy updates, as in exp 68.
